title: Astrid and the Summer
premise: Hazel Whitlock inherits a debt-ridden vineyard and a town that remembers her family's failures better than its wines. When a local literacy charity's anonymous pen-pal program pairs her with a stranger, she pours out her fears — only to discover the letters come from Elias Marchetti, the developer's lawyer sent to seize her land. Falling for him through ink and then in person, Hazel must choose between fighting him in the hearing room and trusting him beyond it; in the end, Elias walks away from the firm, testifies on her behalf, and stays through the first harvest, when the last train out of Alder Creek leaves without him.
about_author: Dominic Oyelaran is a former agricultural journalist who spent three harvest seasons embedded in small vineyard communities before turning to fiction. He writes love stories about people who inherit more trouble than land.

chapters.title: Debts Instead of Grapes
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She arrives at Whitlock Vineyard to bury her estranged father and discovers the estate is mortgaged to its trellises. The emotional beat is grief sharpened by betrayal — she came to inherit a legacy and finds a ledger of losses instead.

chapters.title: The Man from Meridian
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He arrives in Alder Creek representing Meridian Development, tasked with acquiring Whitlock Vineyard for a resort. Charming and ruthless, he charms the town council while privately noting the vineyard's stubborn beauty. The beat is cold ambition meeting an unexpected flicker of doubt.

chapters.title: Letters in a Tin Box
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The town librarian strong-arms Hazel into the charity pen-pal program, promising anonymity and 'no small talk about weather.' Hazel writes her first letter in the cellar among her father's unsold vintages. The beat is guarded loneliness reaching, blindly, toward a stranger.

chapters.title: Correspondent Unknown
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Bored at his rented cottage, Elias joins the same program on a whim and writes with a candor he shows no one. The librarian, mischievous, pairs the two without checking the sign-in sheet. The beat is dramatic irony planted: two enemies beginning to confide.

chapters.title: What the Vine Remembers
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She surveys the vineyard with old foreman Ruthie, learning the land is healthier than the finances. A letter arrives and she answers honestly for the first time in years. The beat is cautious hope — the vineyard, like her heart, might still be alive.

chapters.title: The Hearing Date
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Meridian files foreclosure proceedings with a hearing set for late summer, just before harvest. Elias drafts the strategy but hesitates when he reads Hazel's name on the defendant line. The beat is ambition colliding with the first crack in his armor.

chapters.title: Ink and Honesty
chapters.summary: Alternating letters, both POVs. Over weeks the pen pals exchange confessions — her fear of becoming her father, his weariness with winning for people he despises. The beat is intimacy accelerating past what either intends, each falling for a person they've never seen.

chapters.title: A Dinner for Enemies
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At a town fundraiser, Hazel and Elias meet properly and spar publicly — she recognizes the name from the foreclosure notice. They trade barbed courtesies over bad catered wine. The beat is antagonism with an undertow of attraction both refuse to name.

chapters.title: Rain on the Trellises
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. A storm traps Elias at the vineyard when he comes to serve papers; Hazel, grudgingly, lets him wait it out. They work side by side saving the vines and talk until midnight — real talk, no letters. The beat is the mask slipping for both of them.

chapters.title: The Letter That Gives Him Away
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Rereading her pen pal's letters, Hazel notices phrases Elias used word for word in the rain. She tests him with a quoted line and watches him go pale. The beat is betrayal — the one honest voice in her life belongs to the man destroying her.

chapters.title: Confession, Unsent
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias drafts a letter confessing everything and burns it. His firm grows suspicious of his delays; his boss gives him an ultimatum. The beat is a man trapped between the self he built and the self he's becoming, choosing neither.

chapters.title: Cold Cellar, Colder Words
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel confronts Elias with the letters; he neither denies nor explains, and she orders him off her land. She stops writing entirely, and the librarian's tin box sits unopened. The beat is heartbreak weaponized into resolve — she'll fight the hearing alone.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Testimony
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Preparing for the hearing, Hazel gathers evidence of Meridian's predatory lending and uncovers her father's hidden correspondence with Elias's own late father — an old friendship, and an old debt Meridian owes the Whitlocks. The beat is justice shifting from plea to counterattack.

chapters.title: The Last Train Timetable
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias discovers the firm falsified loan documents and faces disbarment if he exposes them, ruin if he doesn't. He buys a ticket on the last train out of Alder Creek for the night before the hearing, then can't decide whether to board. The beat is the crossroads made literal.

chapters.title: What Hazel Decides
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Ruthie urges Hazel to use the father's letters to destroy Elias along with Meridian. Hazel, reading her pen pal's unsent confession — which Ruthie intercepted and saved — sees his choice mirrored in her own. The beat is mercy chosen over vengeance, at real cost.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, the climax. Elias takes the stand against his own firm, presenting the forged documents and the Whitlock counterclaim; Meridian's case collapses. Hazel testifies last, her voice steady, and when asked about her relationship with opposing counsel, she answers, 'He was my pen pal.' The beat is public ruin and public truth at once.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Ash and Paper
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The vineyard is saved; the town celebrates; Elias, disgraced and unemployed, keeps his distance, unsure of his welcome. Hazel finds him at the station platform, ticket in hand. The beat is the quiet after the storm — victory that feels incomplete without him.

chapters.title: Stay After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. On the platform Hazel asks him, plainly, to stay — not for her, but because the harvest needs hands and the town needs a lawyer who tells the truth. He lets the train leave without him. The beat is the book's central image fulfilled: choosing to remain.

chapters.title: First Pick
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Harvest begins at dawn; the whole town turns out, Elias hauling bins beside Ruthie. Hazel writes one final letter to her pen pal and hands it to him in person. The beat is joy earned through labor — the vineyard's first harvest as a shared inheritance.

chapters.title: The Wine We Keep
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias opens a small law practice above the library and takes the town's cases for what people can pay. He writes back to Hazel, properly this time, signing his name. The beat is a man rebuilding identity on honest ground.

chapters.title: Belonging
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At the harvest festival, Hazel toasts her father — the man he was, not the debts he left — and Elias stands beside her as the town accepts them both. She realizes belonging isn't inherited; it's built, season by season. The beat is reconciliation with the past.

chapters.title: Astrid and the Summer
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, epilogue. Hazel names the vineyard's first bottled blend 'Astrid,' after the grandmother who planted the original vines, and gives the first bottle to Elias. The last image: two glasses on the cellar steps as the season turns. The beat is love in the present tense at last.
